The Atlantic stargazer Uranoscopus scaber attains a maximum standard length of 40 cm [Li = 40 cm], a size that places it among the larger members of the family Uranoscopidae. Specimens collected during trawl surveys along the Mediterranean continental shelf consistently approach this asymptotic dimension, with individuals exceeding 35 cm being recorded predominantly from deeper, cooler waters. This ultimate length is associated with a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 1069 grams [Wwi = 1069 grams], a body mass that reflects the species' robust, dorsoventrally flattened morphology and its energetically costly ambush predatory lifestyle. The length-weight relationship for this species follows the general fish growth pattern, with the asymptotic mass derived from the cubic relationship to standard length. Field observations indicate that growth decelerates markedly once individuals surpass roughly 30 cm, suggesting that resource allocation shifts progressively from somatic expansion towards the maintenance of existing tissues and the accumulation of gonadal products during the later stages of the life history.

Sexual maturation in Uranoscopus scaber is initiated when individuals attain a standard length at puberty of 14 cm [Lp = 14 cm], a size that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of estimated at 45.8 grams [Wwp = estimated at 45.8 grams]. This developmental milestone is reached relatively early in the species' growth trajectory, typically within the first two to three years of life under conditions prevailing in the eastern Atlantic. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from individuals collected across the species' range reveals that the onset of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males coincides closely with this length threshold. The transition to reproductive maturity is accompanied by a pronounced shift in energy expenditure, as the fish begins to invest a substantial portion of its ingested resources into gamete production rather than continued somatic growth, a pattern common among iteroparous benthic marine teleosts with a moderate lifespan.

Neonatal life begins at an exceptionally small scale, with the wet weight at birth of calculated at 0.0042 grams [Wwb = calculated at 0.0042 grams], a mass derived from the estimated egg diameter of two millimeters. The fertilised ova are demersal and adhesive, deposited by the gravid female onto rocky substrates or within crevices, where they are presumably guarded by the male parent until eclosion. The yolk-sac larvae that emerge following chorion rupture are lecithotrophic and remain entirely dependent on endogenous yolk reserves during the first several days post-hatching. During this endotrophic phase, rapid morphological differentiation occurs, including the development of the mouth and the functional differentiation of the digestive tract, preparing the prolarva for the critical transition to first exogenous feeding. The energetic constraints imposed by such a diminutive starting mass likely contribute to high natural mortality rates during the early larval stages, a common bottleneck in the recruitment dynamics of many marine fish species.

Studies conducted under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C] have yielded a maximum lifespan of estimate of 10 years [am = estimate of 10 years] for this species. This longevity is arguably moderate for a teleost of its ultimate body size and is comparable to that recorded for other temperate uranoscopids. The ageing profile suggests that after reaching sexual maturity, individuals typically experience several reproductive seasons before eventually succumbing to senescence-related physiological deterioration. The metabolic rate at the experimental temperature of 18 °C appears to underpin a relatively slow pace of life, with growth rates and gonadal recrudescence occurring at a measured tempo that allows the species to sustain a iteroparous reproductive strategy over nearly a decade. Field validation of this captive longevity estimate remains an ongoing objective for Mediterranean fisheries biologists.

From a comparative ecological perspective, the life history of Uranoscopus scaber reflects a classic trade-off between investment in somatic maintenance and reproductive output. The 40 cm [Li = 40 cm] ultimate standard length and 1069 gram [Wwi = 1069 gram] asymptotic mass are attained only after several years of steady feeding on benthic invertebrates and small fish, a diet that supports the slow but sustained accumulation of body tissues. The 14 cm [Lp = 14 cm] standard length at puberty and the associated wet weight at puberty of 45.8 grams [Wwp = 45.8 grams] indicate that reproduction commences well before maximum size is achieved, a strategy that buffers the population against the high early-life mortality inherent in the species' tiny 0.0042 gram [Wwb = 0.0042 gram] birth mass.
